name: Pale Blue-Green
lede: Pale Blue-Green is a descriptive phrase more than a name, a very light green that the books use for pigments and the standards use for a swatch.

sections.title: A description, not a name
sections.body:
Pale blue-green is a modifier plus a hue, built from [[blue-green]] and a lightening word [1]. The library finds it in Ridgway's 1912 atlas, plate VII, and in ISCC-NBS block 148, which calls the swatch a "very pale green" [1]. Despite the name, it reads as a green, with little blue in it [1].

The phrase does have a real use in the books. Coles describes chrysocolla, a copper mineral found beside malachite and azurite, as a delicate pale blue-green pigment [2]. Traces of it turn up in Twelfth Dynasty Egyptian tombs and in the Kizil wall paintings of Turkistan, and because it is so translucent in oil it works best in watercolor and egg tempera [2]. This swatch is closer to a washed-out [[sea-green]] or [[pale-turquoise]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 21 carry this color over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [3]. In 88 per cent of the 16 paintings where we measured its rank, it plays a light [3]. Six of the matches date from the 1800s, and the earliest is a painting by Bartolomeo di Giovanni of about 1488, a floor not a first [3].
